decision.resolution: [Summary of the 1906 editor’s note.] The editor reports a manuscript of 148 half-written folio pages in the Royal Library in Berlin and notes Steinthal’s use of selected passages in his edition of Humboldt’s language-philosophical works. (1906 Ed.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: subjugation-scope
decision.resolution: “Down to subjugation by Europeans” adopts the temporal reading of German bis auf. “Except for subjugation by Europeans” remains possible; that reading would make subjugation an exception to the claim of freedom from foreign influence. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: american-contact
decision.resolution: The Norse settlement at L’Anse aux Meadows, dating from around 1000 and discovered in 1960, supplies archaeological evidence of pre-Columbian European presence. This qualifies the picture of isolation; it does not by itself establish an influence on American languages. See [Parks Canada](https://www.parcs.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/nl/meadows/culture). (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: nations-or-languages
decision.resolution: “In the languages themselves” interprets a German pronoun that can also refer to the nations. The later “them all” likewise leaves open whether nations or languages are placed on the asserted scale. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: writing-and-literature
decision.resolution: Alphabetic writing is only one kind of writing. Maya script combines word signs and syllable signs; absence of an alphabet therefore does not establish absence of writing. “Literature in the proper sense” and the scale of a “lower level” express Humboldt’s evaluative criterion. See [SLUB Dresden](https://www.slub-dresden.de/en/explore/manuscripts/the-dresden-maya-codex/deciphering). (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: parts-of-presentation
decision.resolution: “The most important parts” is taken to mean parts of the presentation. The German possessive also permits parts of the individual languages; its form does not settle the reference. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: sound-designation
decision.resolution: The German Lautbezeichnung can concern designation through sounds or the specification of those sounds. The present rendering follows the former reading; the latter remains possible. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: american-publication
decision.resolution: Humboldt’s larger American project remained unfinished, although he left substantial grammatical studies, including a Nahuatl grammar (modern manuscript-based edition, 1994). The Nahuatl dictionary, published in 2000, was conceived by Humboldt but compiled and revised chiefly by Eduard Buschmann, who continued the work after Humboldt’s death. See [Drechsel 2024, chapters 7–8](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108966801) and [Trabant 2002, §4.2](https://shesl.org/trabant-legs-intempestif/). (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: idiom
decision.resolution: “Idioms” here means individual languages or varieties, rather than idiomatic expressions. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: genus-shift
decision.resolution: The earlier analogy makes individual languages species under the genus of human language. Here each language is itself called a “new genus”: the German repeats Gattung. This apparent shift in classificatory level is retained; “new kind” is another possible reading. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: english-gender
decision.resolution: English distinguishes he, she and it, although nouns are not commonly marked for gender. Humboldt’s claim is therefore too broad if read as excluding every gender distinction; a restriction to nominal gender is possible but is not explicit here. See [English Grammar Today](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/gender). (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: coptic-participle-comparison
decision.resolution: Coptic circumstantial clauses can do work rendered by participles in Greek or English: for example, “He found them sleeping” (Matthew 26:40). See [Plumley, §§197–197a](https://cdn.suscopts.org/files/deacons/coptic/introductory-sahidic-coptic-grammar_john-martin-plumley-1948.pdf); this supports the functional comparison without identifying Humboldt’s precise intended construction. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: greek-article-development
decision.resolution: Greek article forms retain demonstrative uses in Homer alongside emerging article uses; see [Smyth, §§1099–1102](https://grammars.alpheios.net/smyth/xhtml/body.1_div1.4_div2.16.html). The comparison here does not establish a direct derivation of Greek from an Indian language. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: historical-german-passive
decision.resolution: Inflected passive forms are attested in Gothic; Old High German has passive constructions with auxiliaries. “German” is retained here; a broader historical use for Germanic may be intended. See [Lehmann, §5.5](https://lrc.la.utexas.edu/books/pgmc/5-syntax). (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: system-of-languages
decision.resolution: “System of languages” takes the German Sprachsystem in the classificatory context of passage 8. “System of language,” referring to language’s internal organization, is another possible reading. (Trans.)

decision.question: Reader footnote: period

decision.question: Reader footnote: basic-sounds
decision.resolution: “Basic sounds” (Grundlaute) leaves open whether elementary speech sounds or root-like sound formations are in view; it is not a substitution of the modern term phonemes. (Trans.)

decision.authority: Codex coordinator, applying Brett-approved D029 policy under D030; no German specialist or new reader approval claimed
decision.question: Reader footnote: individuality-across-passages
decision.resolution: In passage 5, “true individuality” was tied to specific designation by sounds; here individuality is felt in the language’s working as a whole. The German uses Individualität in both places. These different emphases are retained without imposing a fixed opposition between individuality, distinctive character and character. (Trans.)

decision.question: Reader footnote: substantive-content
